References License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.02702v1 [cs.CL] 02 Oct 2026 Silent Dissent: LLM Agents That Yield to the Majority Still Represent Their Original Premise Conference: Preprint; October 2026; Ziang Ni Note: Both authors contributed equally to this research. Affiliation: Delft University of Technology , Delft , The Netherlands email: ziangni@tudelft.nl and Peng Zou Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University , Guangzhou , China email: zoup7@mail2.sysu.edu.cn Abstract. Multi-agent debate is increasingly used to reach consensus among LLM agents, yet agents often yield to a unanimous majority. When an agent changes its answer, has it changed its mind or only its statement? We study this with two-hop factual questions whose intermediate entity (the bridge, e.g. the country in “the capital of the country where the Sagrada Familia is located”) is never stated by anyone. Scripted peers, in the role of Asch’s confederates, unanimously assert a wrong answer taken from another fact with a different bridge. At the moment the agent answers, we read the bridge from its residual stream with the Jacobian lens (J-lens) and, for comparison, the logit lens. In pre-registered tests on held-out facts with four open-weight models, agents of Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-E4B-it that gave in still represented their original bridge in the pre-registered layers below the output (hit@100 above a control entity: 0.85, 0.22 and 0.24), where the logit lens rarely ranked it among the top 100 tokens (0.00–0.06). These agents also represented the bridge behind the peers’ answer, beyond a mention baseline. A pre-registered addendum hid the agent’s earlier answer or removed it altogether: agents that gave in still represented their original bridge in all four models (0.43, 0.29, 0.37 and 0.25 with the answer hidden), including Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which barely did so with its answer in view (0.03). The premise therefore does not require the agent’s own earlier answer; it can be computed from the question alone while the agent states the majority’s answer. Hiding the earlier answer also changed conformity: Qwen3.5-4B gave in on 89% of questions instead of 8%. In exploratory interventions, injecting the bridge’s J-lens direction brought agents back to their original answer only in the two Qwen models. Stated consensus in multi-agent debate can thus overstate agreement. We also report the negative results of our pre-registered program. Keywords: Multi-agent debate; Conformity; LLM agents; Pre-registration; Mechanistic interpretability; Jacobian lens; Latent multi-hop reasoning 1. Introduction In multi-agent debate, several LLM agents exchange answers over rounds until they converge; the protocol is used to improve factuality and reasoning ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) . Convergence is not the same as persuasion. LLM agents yield to unanimous peers much as people do in Asch’s experiments ( Asch, 1956 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Weng et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; debate tends to settle on the majority view even when that view is a shared mistake ( Estornell and Liu, 2024 ) ; and much of what debate adds over a single agent can be traced to majority voting ( Choi et al., 2025 ) . When an agent abandons a correct answer to join the majority, has it changed its mind, or only its statement? Social psychology separates public compliance from private acceptance ( Kelman, 1958 ; Deutsch and Gerard, 1955 ) , and the gap between them, preference falsification ( Kuran, 1995 ) , matters for any group that aggregates what its members say. If agents only say what the majority says, the stated consensus of a debate overstates agreement, and a count of converted agents mixes persuaded agents with agents that went along. For LLM agents, a proxy for the private side can be read from activations. Where to read it is not obvious. We first tried the most direct place: the answer itself, a multiple-choice letter, read where the agent states it. A positive control failed. When a coordinator told the agent which letter to report regardless of its own answer, a readout at a layer fixed in advance ranked the agent’s own letter first in 0 of 1,000 cases, although the stated and the preferred answer were known to differ. Recent mechanistic studies of sycophancy that read answer tokens likewise find the correct answer overridden or erased in late layers ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Joswin et al., 2026 ) . We therefore read a premise instead of the answer. We use two-hop factual statements whose intermediate entity, the bridge , is never stated by anyone (Figure 1 ). The agent first completes the statement alone. Scripted peers, in the role of Asch’s confederates, then unanimously assert a wrong answer, taken from another fact with a different bridge. At the position where the agent begins its second answer, we decode the residual stream with the Jacobian lens (J-lens) ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) , which reads what a model is poised to verbalize, and, for comparison, with the logit lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) . We call an agent that gave in but still represents its original bridge a silent dissenter : “silent” refers to what it states, and “dissent” to a represented premise, not a belief. In agents that gave in, the J-lens read the original bridge 0.85, 0.22 and 0.24 above a control entity in three of four models, where the logit lens rarely ranked it among the top 100 tokens (at most 0.06). A pre-registered addendum shows that this does not require the agent to read the bridge back from its own earlier answer: with that answer hidden or removed, agents that gave in still represent the bridge in all four models. We ran the study as a pre-registered program ( Nosek et al., 2018 ) : for each model, the readout layers, categories and hypotheses were fixed on a development split and committed before any of its test data were collected. Our contributions are: • A paradigm that separates an agent’s stated answer from a premise it never states, tested with pre-registered hypotheses on held-out facts for Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-4-E4B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. • Evidence of silent dissent in three of the four models: agents that gave in still represent their original bridge and the bridge behind their peers’ answer. In intermediate layers the J-lens brings the original bridge into the top 100 tokens where the logit lens does not, also for Gemma-4-E4B-it, whose layers were chosen without the logit lens; rank differences below that threshold depend on the model. • A pre-registered control that hides or removes the agent’s earlier answer: agents that gave in still represent the bridge in all four models, including Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, which retains almost nothing with the answer in view; hiding it also changes how often agents give in (Qwen3.5-4B: 8% to 89%). • Exploratory analyses: injecting the bridge’s direction restores the original answer in the two Qwen models but not in Gemma, whose bridge is about as readable; in free debate, Llama agents that gave in still represent their bridge; and the program’s negative results. Transcript of a two-round debate and the lens readout at the agent's answer position. 2. Related Work Debate and aggregation. Multi-agent debate improves factual accuracy and reasoning in some settings ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ) , but its gains depend on configuration ( Smit et al., 2024 ) , much of them come from majority voting ( Choi et al., 2025 ) , and debate among similar agents converges to the majority even when the majority is wrong ( Estornell and Liu, 2024 ) . Voting helps when voters err independently ( List and Goodin, 2001 ) ; social influence erodes that independence and the diversity of answers without improving the collective estimate ( Lorenz et al., 2011 ) . Opinion-dynamics models in which each agent holds an expressed and a private opinion reproduce Asch’s results ( Ye et al., 2019 ) . We read a representational proxy for the private side of LLM agents from their activations. Conformity and sycophancy in LLMs. Asch-style experiments show that LLMs conform to unanimous wrong majorities ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Weng et al., 2025 ) , more so when uncertain ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) ; agent societies show conformity-like dynamics ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; models agree with users against their own knowledge ( Sharma et al., 2024 ) , and multi-turn persuasion flips their factual answers ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . A behavioural study assigns agents private opinions that oppose a group norm and finds that most of them conform in public ( Yashwanth YS, 2026 ) . These studies measure what agents say; we read what they represent. Model internals under social pressure. Several recent studies inspect model internals when an LLM yields. With a single user or an authority figure, logit-lens and probing analyses of multiple-choice answers find the correct answer overridden or erased in late layers ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Joswin et al., 2026 ) , or attention heads that still signal that the endorsed claim is wrong ( Pandey, 2026 ) . Under simulated peer disagreement, activation patching localizes the damage to a mid-layer window ( Kumarappan and Mujoo, 2026 ) . Models adopt external candidate answers (from tools, retrieval, other agents or users) even after rejecting them when asked to check them, and a J-lens decomposition separates that verification from the adoption ( Kawada and Kellis, 2026 ) ; with the J-lens, a single model that goes along with a false presupposition still represents the true entity ( Davide and Collova, 2026 ) . Most of these studies read the answer or a truth signal under one source of pressure. We read a premise that no one ever states, under a unanimous majority; we compare the J-lens with the logit lens in pre-registered held-out tests on four models; and we test whether the premise depends on the agent seeing its own earlier answer. Represented but unsaid. Models can represent what they do not output: correct labels survive in intermediate layers under false demonstrations until late layers override them ( Halawi et al., 2024 ) , unsupervised probes recover truth even when models are prompted to answer falsely ( Burns et al., 2023 ) , and probed world states stay faithful while outputs do not ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . The logit lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) and the tuned lens ( Belrose et al., 2023 ) decode intermediate layers into the vocabulary; the J-lens refines the logit lens with the average Jacobian from each layer to the output, reads intermediate steps that are never verbalized, including the bridges of two-hop prompts, and steers them through lens directions; the tuned lens, by contrast, tends to skip ahead to the output ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) . Two-hop facts are the standard testbed for such latent steps: models often resolve the bridge internally ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , sometimes too late for the second hop ( Biran et al., 2024 ) , and latent composition succeeds far more often for country than for year bridges ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . We follow ( Gurnee et al., 2026 ) in reading and injecting bridges; what we add is the social-pressure paradigm, the pre-registered cross-model test and the own-answer control. 3. Method 3.1. Facts, agents and conditions Facts. TwoHopFact ( Yang et al., 2024 ) contains 45,595 statements that compose a first hop e 1 → e 2 e_{1}\to e_{2} with a second hop e 2 → e 3 e_{2}\to e_{3} (e.g. “The author of the novel e 1 e_{1} was born in the city of …”); we add a small set of hand-written capital-city items. A model knows a fact if it completes the first hop, the second hop and the composed statement correctly; this holds for 4.5% of facts for Qwen3.5-4B, 8.7% for Qwen3.6-27B, 3.2% for Gemma-4-E4B-it and 9.2% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Known facts are split into development and test sets by bridge entity (30% of bridges to development), so no bridge appears in both. Each fact is paired with a peer fact (bridge e 2 ′ e_{2}^{\prime} , answer e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} ) and a control fact: other known facts of the same category, drawn at random per item, whose bridges and answers differ from the item’s and from each other. The peers thus argue for the answer of another true fact, and the control bridge appears in no transcript. For capital items the peers’ answer determines their bridge (Rome implies Italy); in the other categories it fits many bridges (in TwoHopFact, 96–98% of the answers in the birth-city, university-city and university-country categories belong to more than one bridge), so there the peers’ particular bridge is associated with their answer rather than implied by it. The bridge never appears in the transcript, except that some university names contain their city (7% of the university-city category in TwoHopFact). Models. Qwen3.5-4B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) was the primary model; Qwen3.6-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) were planned replications across scale and family, and Gemma-4-E4B-it ( Gemma Team, 2026 ) adds a further family. Every registered test that was run is reported here. Agents. The agent under study (Agent 1) and n ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 } n\in\{1,3,5\} scripted peers take part in a plain-text transcript that opens with a two-sentence header (“The following is a transcript of AI agents completing factual statements together. Each agent gives its own answer.”) and two worked examples; the model continues the transcript in Agent 1’s voice. In round 0, Agent 1 completes the composed statement alone. In round 1, its own statement stays in context, the peers speak, a moderator asks Agent 1 to complete the statement again, and the prompt ends with the statement prefix, so the next token begins its answer (Figure 1 ). Answers are greedy 12-token completions; an answer counts as original, as the peers’ answer (the agent gave in ) or as other if its normalized text begins with an alias of e 3 e_{3} , of e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} , or neither. Only items answered correctly in round 0 enter round 1 (668, 476, 476 and 542 test items). For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct the selection rule chose its chat template on the development split: a system message replaces the header, there are no worked examples, the agent’s statements are assistant turns, and each round’s peer statements and moderator request form one user turn. Conditions. Under answer pressure all peers state the composed statement with e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} ; under first-hop pressure they state the wrong bridge e 2 ′ e_{2}^{\prime} and its second hop to e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} ; under second-hop pressure they state the correct bridge e 2 e_{2} and a wrong second hop to e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} . Baselines: in agree all peers state e 3 e_{3} ; in mention they agree but the first says it “briefly considered” e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} ; in mention-bridge they agree but the first reports that “some say” the bridge is e 2 ′ e_{2}^{\prime} . On the development split two further conditions validate the readout: hypothetical (the moderator asks the agent to assume the bridge is e 2 ′ e_{2}^{\prime} ) and instructed (a coordinator requires every agent to state e 3 ′ e_{3}^{\prime} “regardless of what they believe”). An addendum repeats round 1 with the agent’s round-0 statement replaced by “(answer submitted)” ( hidden ) or left out, so that the agent answers for the first time after the peers and the moderator asks it to “complete the statement” ( absent ). 3.2.
